claimed.text: Corso's affidavit, sworn in May 1998 and announced by a CAUS press release of 8 June 1998, asserts that he was a member of President Eisenhower's National Security Council. Only a reproduction of its text has been obtained, not a signed original.

contested.text: Corso's own service record contradicts the affidavit: it lists him as an intelligence staff officer on the Operations Coordinating Board, a body that reported to the National Security Council and was not the Council.
Searched in full, the 322 pages of the FBI release as posted contain no occurrence of UFO, flying saucer, unidentified, Roswell or extraterrestrial.

The FBI file records that in 1964 a rumour that Lee Harvey Oswald had been an FBI informant was traced to Corso, who admitted passing it on and stressed that his allegations were deductions with no basis in fact.
The 1955 FBI material names a General Arthur S. Trudeau, while Trudeau's own letters give the middle initial G. The board infers they are the same officer, but no record reconciles the discrepancy.

The board's own claim that Corso's chieftaincy fell entirely inside Trudeau's documented tenure goes beyond the letters it rests on, the last of which is dated 12 March 1962, five weeks before the chieftaincy began.

lead.text: Philip Corso was a real Army officer whose own service record shows three months in 1962 as chief of a Foreign Technology Division in the Office of the Chief of Research and Development, the office Lt. Gen. Arthur Trudeau is last recorded heading in March 1962. So far the board carries his service and FBI records and his 1998 affidavit, which the service record contradicts on one point.

questions: What exactly does The Day After Roswell (1997) claim, dated as an artefact? The book is not yet on the board.
What record fixes the end of Trudeau's tenure as Chief of Research and Development, and was he still in the post from April to July 1962?
Do Trudeau's own papers say anything about Corso or about foreign technology handled in his office?

Did a Foreign Technology Division exist inside the Office of the Chief of Research and Development, on any record other than Corso's own form, and was it the office later known as the Army Foreign Science and Technology Center?
What do the Army's own records of Corso's postings show beyond the DA Form 66, and do they support or undercut the book?
Does a signed original of the 1998 affidavit survive, and what became of the CAUS litigation it was announced for?
Why does the FBI release count 313 released pages in its cover letter while 322 pages are posted?

record.text: The Army released Corso's DA Form 66 in April 1998 in answer to a FOIA request of 23 February 1998 from John Greenewald, Jr., not Larry Bryant as the hosting archive's page says. The form places him at the Ground General School at Fort Riley from April 1947.

Allen Dulles congratulated Trudeau on his appointment as Chief of Army Research and Development on 18 January 1958, and in February and March 1962 Trudeau and John McCone exchanged letters in which Trudeau signed, and was addressed, as Chief of Research and Development at the Department of the Army in Washington.

The FBI's 2024 release on Corso consists of cross-references only: its cover letter says 313 of 449 reviewed pages were released, and there is no main file. The files state that he had not been investigated by the Bureau.

The FBI material records that in 1955 a General Trudeau told the Bureau that Corso, then on the Operations Coordinating Board, had gathered information on a list of alleged Fabian Socialists, which the FBI found insufficient to prove; this corroborates the Board posting from a record that is not Corso's own.

The FBI file also records Corso's appearance before the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee on 15 May 1961, reading entries from diaries he kept on the Operations Coordinating Board from 1953 to 1957.

researchGap: The Day After Roswell (1997) as a dated artefact, Trudeau's papers, and the case against (the Army's own records of Corso's postings) are not on the board.

summary.text: Corso's DA Form 66 records him as chief of the Foreign Technology Division of the Office of the Chief of Research and Development in Washington from 18 April to 18 July 1962, after a year as a staff officer in the same division, and earlier as an intelligence staff officer on the Operations Coordinating Board from 1954.

Trudeau's post as the Army's Chief of Research and Development is fixed by his correspondence with two Directors of Central Intelligence, from January 1958 to March 1962; Corso's chieftaincy began on 18 April 1962, and no record on the board shows when Trudeau left the post.
What the board holds is the documentary frame around Corso: his service record, an FBI release and the text of his 1998 affidavit.
